eligibility.evidence: Methods and Experiments 1-2 (pp.2-4): sentence-verification and category-based induction tests modelled on Rips et al. 1973, Rosch 1973, Osherson et al. 1990, using Rosch 1975 typicality ratings; GPT/GPT-2 (generative) plus masked LMs queried via log-probabilities.

A.title: Do language models learn typicality judgments from text?
A.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2021; arXiv preprint of accepted manuscript)

paradigms.name: Taxonomic sentence verification (typicality effect: 'A X is a Y', log-probability of category word)
paradigms.source_paper: Rips, Shoben & Smith 1973; Rosch 1973; Rosch 1975 ratings
paradigms.location: Experiment 1 and Stimuli Setup, pp.2-3; Table 1 p.1 (565 items, 10 categories)

paradigms.name: Category-based induction (typicality of premise item; nonce-property premise-conclusion pairs)
paradigms.source_paper: Rips 1975; Osherson, Smith, Wilkie, Lopez & Shafir 1990
paradigms.location: Experiment 2, pp.3-4 (12,180 premise-conclusion pairs, nonce properties such as dax)

D.population: native English speakers in Rosch 1975 norming study (goodness-of-example ratings, 10 categories)
D.metric: Rosch 1975 typicality ratings (1-7); Spearman rho with LM log-probabilities; typical vs atypical median split

E.headline: LMs show modest but non-zero sensitivity to typicality in both tests, less extreme than humans; text exposure alone seems insufficient to acquire typicality knowledge.

G.notes: Models are scored by log-probability, no sampling. Per-model correlations appear only in figures, so no model_es. Masked LMs and a 5-gram baseline are excluded from B; their results are pooled in the text ranges. Exact checkpoint identifiers not given. Premise shuffling and property-repeat controls enter as regression covariates.
